messages.subject: Non-stationary-binomial response
parts:
Dear all,

I'm trying to implement a spatial non-stationary model using a binomial response. I'm adapting a piece of code from Ingebrigtsen, Lindgren, and Steinsland (2014), where the response is precipitation (gaussian), to Gambia's malaria cases dataset from the geoR package, which is explained in Moraga (2020). I'm aware that the selection of hyperparameters values is crucial in this kind of model, and the ones I'm using (corresponding to the original paper) are not proper for the selected data, but I'm also sure that there are other silly mistakes. I will appreciate it if you can point these out for me in order to achieve the estimation. I will also appreciate any recommendations for the selection of hyperparameter values, considering that the original priors are very informative. The following code corresponds to the model fitting step, but I'm attaching the complete code with the necessary data in order to reproduce the example. Thank you in advance for your help an guidance.

# Non-stationary:
formula.ns = y ~ -1 +
  f(intercept, 
    model = "linear", 
    mean.linear = 0, 
    prec.linear = 0.0001) +
  f(elevation, 
  model = "linear", 
  mean.linear = 0, 
  prec.linear = 0.0001) +
  f(field, model = spde.ns)

result.ns = inla(formula.ns,
                 family = "binomial",
                 Ntrials = numtrials,
                 data = inla.stack.data(data.stack),
                 control.predictor = list(
A = inla.stack.A(data.stack), 
compute = TRUE, 
link = 1),
                 control.compute = list(cpo = TRUE, 
                                        dic = TRUE),
                 control.family = list(link = "logit"),
                 #control.family = list(hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "loggamma", param = c(2,0.02)))),
                 control.inla = list(h = 1e-4, 
                                     tolerance = 1e-8),
                 verbose = TRUE
)

The specific way the covariate affects the parameter has to be checked which is sensible for your data. In the example in the book, I did such standardization according to what I wanted the final combination to be. For a small number of trials, Binomial data are weakly informative, particularly for second-order properties.

Elias
On Mon, 1 Apr 2024 at 00:12, manjagoc <man...@gmail.com> wrote:

Thank you for the response. So if I define a covariate as  a linear expression (like in your book, you use (mesh$loc[,1] - 5) / 10) should I get better estimates if I change the values of theta? I tried it but still theta estimations seems anchored to prior mean specification (0).

For real data application, besides checking that the covariates vary smoothly over the space as you mentioned before, is there other characteristics that I should check in order to guarantee precise estimations?

El domingo, 31 de marzo de 2024 a las 1:44:35 UTC-6, Elias T. Krainski escribió:
One important point is the link between the parameters (range, marginal variance) and the covariate. Consider the user-friendly parameterization range(s) = exp( some linear predictor ). In this case, the effect of theta on the parameter is non-linear. Therefore changing from -0.5 to -1.5 makes a huge difference on the actual parameters. I added code in the previous script sent to plot the parameter as a function of the covariate to visualize it.
